Both integrate changes from one branch into another. Different history shapes.

## Merge

```
      A---B---C  feature
     /         \
D---E---F---G---H  main (merge commit H)
```

Creates merge commit. Preserves exact history — who branched when, when things joined. Non-destructive.

## Rebase

```
              A'--B'--C'  feature (replayed on top of G)
             /
D---E---F---G  main
```

Replays commits on top of target. Linear history. No merge commit. **Rewrites commit SHAs** — A becomes A'.

---

## When to use each

**Merge:**
- Shared/public branches — never rewrite history others depend on
- Want to preserve "this feature was developed in parallel" context
- Long-lived feature branches with many contributors
- `main` ← `feature` integrations

**Rebase:**
- Local cleanup before PR — squash/reorder your own commits
- Keep feature branch current with main during development
- Want clean linear history for bisect/log readability
- Solo work not yet pushed

---

## Key tradeoffs

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | True, branchy | Clean, linear |
| Safe on shared? | Yes | No — rewrites SHAs |
| Conflicts | Once | Per replayed commit |
| Bisect-friendly | Harder | Easier |
| Context preserved | Yes | Lost (branch point gone) |

---

**Golden rule:** Never rebase commits already pushed to shared branch. Others' history breaks.

Practical pattern: rebase local feature onto main to stay current, merge (or squash-merge) into main when done.
